bibliography.abstract: Understanding how the built environment shapes metro-integrated dockless bike-sharing (DBS) is important for improving first-/last-mile accessibility and sustainable urban mobility. Existing studies often rely on fixed geometric buffers, which can misrepresent the actual spatial footprints of feeder cycling. Using Chengdu as a case study, this paper introduces an Adaptive Catchment Area (ACA) derived from observed DBS origin–destination trajectories and combines it with Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR) and a heat-weighted sensitivity analysis to examine station-level built-environment correlates across morning and evening peaks. The results show that these correlates are spatially heterogeneous and scale-dependent. Fine-grained street connectivity and human-scale street greenery are associated with stronger metro-integrated cycling, while development intensity exhibits a double-edged role by generating demand but also intensifying station-front friction. Employment-related destinations also differ functionally: general workplaces tend to be positively associated with integration, whereas high-end office clusters are more likely to suppress it in some areas. A practitioner interview is used as contextual triangulation to support the interpretation of these spatial patterns and their governance implications. Overall, the study contributes a transferable ACA-based analytical framework for diagnosing station-area feeder-cycling environments while interpreting the empirical findings with appropriate temporal caution.
bibliography.title: The role of urban built environment in promoting dockless bike-sharing and metro integration: an adaptive catchment area approach

en.caveats: The empirical findings are based on a single case study of Chengdu and require temporal caution when generalizing to other urban contexts.
en.what: The study introduces an Adaptive Catchment Area (ACA) framework based on actual dockless bike-sharing trajectories to analyze how the built environment influences first- and last-mile integration with the metro system in Chengdu. Using Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression and heat-weighted sensitivity analysis, it measures the impact of street connectivity, greenery, development intensity, and employment types across morning and evening peak hours.
en.why: It replaces arbitrary, fixed-radius geometric buffers with actual, data-driven cycling footprints, revealing that high-end office clusters can suppress metro-bike integration while general workplaces and human-scale street greenery enhance it.
